Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- Amid high emotions and tight security, thousands lined the streets of Beirut Friday to honor Antoine Ghanem, the anti-Syrian Lebanese MP killed in a powerful bomb blast along with four others. Amin Gemayel (R), Phalange party head, carries the coffin of assassinated deputy Antoine Ghamen. Against an atmosphere of intense political and patriotic fervor, the flag-draped coffins of the politician and two bodyguards also killed in Wednesday's rush hour blast made its way through the city's Christian district to the Sacred Heart church on what the government had declared as a day of national mourning. The procession was accompanied by thousands waving flags, as well as a brass band playing the anthem of Ghanem's Phalange Party, The Associated Press reported . TV pictures showed distraught mourners crowding and reaching out to the coffins as they were carried aloft. Several people were seen to collapse and had to be carried away. Mourners also carried photographs, threw rose petals and unfurled banners, some of which read "We Won't Kneel," AP said. The coffins were greeted at the Christian Maronite church with applause from the gathered mourners, the agency said, including majority leaders and the Lebanese cabinet as well as Ghanem's family and friends. Ghanem was later buried in the city's Christian district. Ghanem's death is the latest in a series of attacks targeting prominent anti-Syrian figures, with the most notorious being the February 2005 assassination in Beirut of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, which sparked widespread protests that led to the ouster of Syrian forces from Lebanon. Hariri also died in a massive explosion. The incident threatens to cast the country into political uncertainty ahead of a key presidential vote in a tightly divided parliament, almost evenly split between anti- and pro-Syrian camps.  Watch how Ghanem's death disrupts Lebanese politics » . CNN's Beirut bureau chief Brent Sadler said that many Lebanese now feared for the future, especially given other events in the region including the conflict between Palestinians and Israelis, recent political differences in Iraq and Iran's bid to become a super power. "There continues to be among a great deal of people here a sense of foreboding that perhaps the worst is yet to come," he said. U.S. President George W. Bush, in a written statement, joined other world leaders in condemning the "horrific assassination." "Since October 2004, there has been a tragic pattern of political assassinations and attempted assassinations designed to silence those Lebanese who courageously defend their vision of an independent and democratic Lebanon," Bush said Wednesday. Also in a written statement, a spokesperson for Ban Ki-moon said the U.N. secretary-general "condemns in the strongest terms this terrorist attack." "The secretary general urges all Lebanese to exercise utmost calm and restraint at this very critical time and to allow judicial procedures to take their course," the spokesperson said. Bush's statement added: "The United States opposes any attempts to intimidate the Lebanese people as they seek to exercise their democratic right to select a president without foreign interference. We will continue to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the Lebanese people as they resist attempts by the Syrian and Iranian regimes and their allies to destabilize Lebanon and undermine its sovereignty." The U.S. Embassy in Beirut issued a statement saying: "It is not a coincidence that these attacks target those figures who have been working to secure Lebanon's independence from renewed Syrian hegemony. We note with concern that many Lebanese politicians allied with Syria have in fact warned that murder and violence would be the results of any effort to exercise genuine parliamentary democracy." And U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, in a written statement, said: "The bombing that claimed these lives was another act in a campaign of terror by those who want to turn back the clock on Lebanon's hard-won democratic gains." "The world should speak with one voice in calling for an end to violence in Lebanon intended to subvert democratic processes in that country," Rice said. "Lebanese elections, scheduled to begin in just days, must proceed, in accordance with the Constitution, without threats of foreign interference and the violence that accompanies such obstruction." BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) — Amid heightened emotion and stringent security measures, thousands of mourners lined the streets of Beirut on Friday to pay tribute to Antoine Ghanem, the anti-Syrian Lebanese member of parliament killed alongside four others in a powerful bomb blast.

Amin Gemayel, head of the Phalange Party, was seen carrying the coffin of the assassinated deputy. Amid an atmosphere charged with political and patriotic fervor, the flag-draped coffins of the slain politician and the two bodyguards who perished with him in Wednesday's rush-hour explosion were borne through the city's Christian district to the Sacred Heart church, on a day the government had officially designated for national mourning.

The funeral procession was accompanied by thousands of flag-waving citizens and a brass band performing the anthem of Ghanem's Phalange Party, according to the Associated Press. Television footage captured grief-stricken mourners pressing forward to reach the coffins as they were carried above the crowd; several individuals were seen collapsing and had to be carried away for assistance. Mourners also held aloft photographs of the deceased, scattered rose petals, and unfurled banners—some bearing the defiant message "We Won't Kneel," the AP reported.

The coffins were received at the Christian Maronite church with applause from those assembled, including majority leaders, members of the Lebanese cabinet, and Ghanem's family and friends, according to the agency. Ghanem was subsequently laid to rest in the city's Christian quarter.

Ghanem's assassination represents the latest in a string of attacks targeting prominent anti-Syrian figures, the most infamous being the February 2005 assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri in Beirut—an event that ignited widespread protests culminating in the withdrawal of Syrian forces from Lebanon. Hariri, too, perished in a massive explosion.

This latest incident threatens to plunge the country into political uncertainty as it approaches a pivotal presidential vote within a parliament sharply divided between pro- and anti-Syrian factions.

Watch how Ghanem's death disrupts Lebanese politics »

CNN's Beirut bureau chief, Brent Sadler, observed that many Lebanese now harbor deep concerns about the nation's future, particularly in light of broader regional developments—including the ongoing Israeli-Palestinian conflict, political tensions in Iraq, and Iran's aspirations toward regional dominance. "There continues to be among a great deal of people here a sense of foreboding that perhaps the worst is yet to come," he said.

U.S. President George W. Bush, in a written statement, joined other world leaders in condemning the "horrific assassination." "Since October 2004, there has been a tragic pattern of political assassinations and attempted assassinations designed to silence those Lebanese who courageously defend their vision of an independent and democratic Lebanon," Bush stated on Wednesday.

In a separate written statement, a spokesperson for U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon declared that Ban "condemns in the strongest terms this terrorist attack," adding that the secretary-general "urges all Lebanese to exercise utmost calm and restraint at this very critical time and to allow judicial procedures to take their course."

Bush's statement further noted: "The United States opposes any attempts to intimidate the Lebanese people as they seek to exercise their democratic right to select a president without foreign interference. We will continue to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the Lebanese people as they resist attempts by the Syrian and Iranian regimes and their allies to destabilize Lebanon and undermine its sovereignty."

The U.S. Embassy in Beirut released a statement asserting: "It is not a coincidence that these attacks target those figures who have been working to secure Lebanon's independence from renewed Syrian hegemony. We note with concern that many Lebanese politicians allied with Syria have in fact warned that murder and violence would be the results of any effort to exercise genuine parliamentary democracy."

U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, in her own written statement, remarked: "The bombing that claimed these lives was another act in a campaign of terror by those who want to turn back the clock on Lebanon's hard-won democratic gains." She further emphasized, "The world should speak with one voice in calling for an end to violence in Lebanon intended to subvert democratic processes in that country. Lebanese elections, scheduled to begin in just days, must proceed, in accordance with the Constitution, without threats of foreign interference and the violence that accompanies such obstruction."

**Beirut Funeral Draws Thousands as Lebanon Mourns Slain Lawmaker Antoine Ghanem**

*By CNN Staff*

BEIRUT, Lebanon — Thousands of mourners flooded the streets of Beirut's Achrafieh district Friday for the funeral of Antoine Ghanem, the Lebanese member of parliament killed in a car bombing earlier this week, in a ceremony that underscored the deepening political crisis gripping the country.

Ghanem, a Christian legislator aligned with the anti-Syrian March 14 coalition, was one of nine people killed when a massive explosive device tore through his motorcade in the Sin el-Fil neighborhood as he returned from a trip abroad. His death marked the latest in a string of assassinations targeting anti-Syrian politicians and journalists since 2005, further destabilizing a nation already reeling from political paralysis.

**A Procession Through Grief and Anger**

The funeral procession began at Beirut's Mar Mikhael Church, where Ghanem's flag-draped coffin was carried by supporters chanting slogans against Syria and calling for justice. Mourners, many waving Lebanese flags and holding portraits of the slain MP, packed the narrow streets leading to the cemetery, some weeping openly while others shouted denunciations of what they called a campaign of terror against Lebanon's sovereignty.

Security was extraordinarily tight, with Lebanese army units and riot police forming a heavy cordon around the route amid fears of further violence. Snipers were reportedly positioned on rooftops as helicopters circled overhead.

Prominent figures from the March 14 alliance, including Druze leader Walid Jumblatt and Christian politician Samir Geagea, joined the procession, their presence a show of unity among factions opposed to Syrian influence in Lebanese affairs. Saad Hariri, leader of the parliamentary majority bloc and son of assassinated former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, delivered emotional remarks, vowing that the killings would not derail the country's push for independence.

"They think that by killing us one by one, they will silence us," Hariri told the crowd, his voice breaking. "They are wrong. Every drop of blood spilled makes us more determined."

**A Nation on Edge**

Ghanem's assassination came at a particularly precarious moment for Lebanon, with parliament set to elect a new president in the coming weeks — a vote that has become a flashpoint in the struggle between the pro-Western governing coalition and the Hezbollah-led opposition backed by Syria and Iran.

His death reduces the parliamentary majority's numbers, raising fears among his allies that the killings are part of a deliberate strategy to tip the balance of power ahead of the presidential vote. Since 2005, at least half a dozen anti-Syrian figures — including journalist Samir Kassir, politician George Hawi, and MP Pierre Gemayel — have been killed in similar attacks, none of which have resulted in prosecutions.

"This is not just an assassination of one man," said one mourner, a schoolteacher who gave her name only as Nadine. "This is an assassination of our future, of our right to choose our own destiny."

**International Condemnation**

The killing drew swift condemnation from governments around the world. The White House issued a statement calling the assassination "a cowardly act aimed at undermining Lebanon's democracy and sovereignty," while French President Nicolas Sarkozy urged the international community to redouble efforts to protect Lebanon's political process.

United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon called for an "urgent and thorough investigation," reiterating support for the U.N.-backed tribunal established to prosecute those responsible for the 2005 assassination of Rafik Hariri, an investigation many believe is linked to the broader wave of killings.

Syria, which withdrew its troops from Lebanon in 2005 after nearly three decades of military and political dominance, has repeatedly denied any involvement in the assassinations. A statement from the Syrian Foreign Ministry called the accusations "baseless and politically motivated," urging Lebanese authorities to look elsewhere for the perpetrators.

Israel, too, condemned the attack, with a spokesperson for the prime minister's office saying that "those seeking to sow chaos in Lebanon are enemies of peace and stability in the entire region."

**A Fragile Path Forward**

As the coffin was lowered into the ground at a private ceremony attended by Ghanem's family, questions loomed over Lebanon's ability to hold together amid the mounting violence. With parliament already delayed multiple times in its effort to select a new head of state, analysts warn that further attacks could plunge the country into deeper crisis — or worse, renewed conflict.

For now, Beirut remains a city marked by mourning and defiance, its streets lined with photographs of the dead and its politicians vowing, again, that they will not be intimidated.

"We bury our friend today," Hariri said, "but we do not bury our cause."

*CNN's Beirut bureau contributed to this report.*

Antoine Ghanem, a Lebanese member of parliament, was killed in a car bomb attack in Beirut. The UN also weighed in on the assassination:

- **UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon** condemned the attack, expressing concern over the ongoing violence targeting Lebanese political figures.
- The UN reiterated calls for those responsible for this and previous assassinations (including the 2005 killing of former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri) to be brought to justice.
- The killing renewed international attention on the UN-backed tribunal investigating political assassinations in Lebanon, and calls were made to expand its mandate to cover the broader string of killings targeting anti-Syrian politicians and journalists.

## Funeral Proceedings
Ghanem's funeral became a significant political event, drawing large crowds from the anti-Syrian March 14 coalition. Attendees and speakers used the occasion to:

- Reaffirm commitment to Lebanese sovereignty and independence from Syrian influence
- Call for the presidential election to proceed despite intimidation
- Demand international support for identifying and prosecuting those responsible

# Thousands Mourn Slain Lebanese Lawmaker Antoine Ghanem in Beirut Funeral

**BEIRUT** — Thousands of mourners gathered in Beirut this week for the funeral of Antoine Ghanem, a Christian member of parliament from the anti-Syrian March 14 coalition, who was killed along with six others in a car bomb attack in the Sin al-Fil district. The assassination has plunged Lebanon deeper into political crisis, coming just weeks before parliament was due to elect a new president.

Ghanem's coffin, draped in the Lebanese flag, was carried through crowds of grieving supporters who chanted anti-Syrian slogans and called for justice, echoing scenes that have become tragically familiar in a country scarred by a string of political killings since 2005. Many in the crowd carried photographs of Ghanem alongside images of previously assassinated figures, including former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, journalist Gebran Tueni, and MP Pierre Gemayel — all seen by their allies as victims of a campaign to silence voices opposed to Syrian influence in Lebanon.

"Every time we bury one of our leaders, we bury a piece of our hope for an independent Lebanon," said one mourner, echoing sentiments widely shared among the anti-Syrian bloc, which has repeatedly accused Damascus of orchestrating the killings — a charge Syria has consistently denied.

The assassination drew swift condemnation from world leaders. U.S. President George W. Bush called it "a reprehensible act of terrorism" aimed at destabilizing Lebanon's fragile democracy, adding that "the United States remains committed to helping the Lebanese people defend their sovereignty and their right to choose their own leaders, free from foreign interference and intimidation."

Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice echoed that message, stating that the killing was "a cowardly attempt to derail Lebanon's democratic process" and reaffirming that "those seeking to sow chaos and fear will not succeed in silencing the voices of the Lebanese people."

# A Nation Mourns: Thousands Gather for Slain Lebanese Lawmaker

*Beirut* — The streets of Beirut fell silent this morning save for the rhythmic chanting of mourners and the distant toll of church bells, as tens of thousands of Lebanese citizens converged on the capital to bid farewell to a member of parliament whose car was torn apart by a roadside bomb earlier this week.

"I brought my children so they would understand what sacrifice means," said Nadia Khoury, a schoolteacher from the Ashrafieh district, clutching the hands of two young boys dressed in their Sunday clothes. "We are burying a man, but we refuse to bury the truth."

The coffin, draped in the Lebanese flag, was carried through streets lined with portraits of previous political figures who met similar fates in recent years—a grim gallery that has become tragically familiar to residents of a country still reckoning with the legacy of foreign intervention and internal fracture.

## Eyewitness Accounts

Elderly shopkeeper Georges Fares, who watched the procession from the shuttered entrance of his stationery store, recalled the sound of the explosion days earlier. "The windows shook three streets away. I knew immediately—we all knew immediately—what kind of message was being sent, and to whom."

Near the square's edge, university students had formed a human chain, their arms linked as a symbolic barrier against what many described as a climate of fear. "They think killing one voice silences a movement," said Rami Aoun, a political science student. "Instead, look around you. This is not silence."

Some mourners wept openly; others stood in stony, disciplined silence, their jaws set with an anger that seemed to simmer just beneath the surface of grief.

## Political Context

The assassinated MP had been a prominent voice calling for full withdrawal of Syrian military influence from Lebanese affairs and had testified before international bodies regarding alleged interference in the country's sovereignty. His killing marks the latest in a series of attacks targeting politicians, journalists, and intellectuals associated with the anti-Syrian coalition that emerged forcefully following the assassination of former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri.

Opposition leaders speaking at the funeral did not mince words. One prominent figure, addressing the crowd from a hastily constructed platform, declared: "Every bomb they detonate only detonates our resolve further. We will complete what our martyrs began."

Representatives from the Free Patriotic Movement, the Lebanese Forces, and other coalition partners stood shoulder to shoulder—a display of unity that observers noted has become both more common and more urgent as the death toll among anti-Syrian figures has risen.

Foreign diplomats, including representatives from France and the United States, were present, their attendance itself a pointed diplomatic statement regarding international concern over Lebanon's fragile stability.

## An Uncertain Road Ahead

As the procession made its way toward the cemetery, chants of "Syria out!" echoed alongside more traditional funeral prayers, the two blending into something that felt less like mourning and more like a declaration.

Whether this latest killing will harden political resolve or deepen the climate of intimidation remains an open question—one that hangs over Beirut like the incense smoke still drifting above Martyrs' Square long after the coffin was lowered into the ground.

For a nation that has buried too many of its voices in recent years, today was not simply a funeral. It was, mourners repeatedly insisted, a referendum on fear itself—and on which side of history Lebanon intends to stand.

# Lebanese Lawmaker Killed in Car Bombing, Deepening Crisis Over Presidential Vote

**BEIRUT, Lebanon (AP)** — A car bomb tore through a residential neighborhood in a Christian suburb of Beirut on Wednesday, killing anti-Syrian lawmaker Antoine Ghanem and at least five others, in an assassination that has plunged Lebanon deeper into political turmoil just weeks before parliament is due to elect a new president.

Ghanem, 64, a member of the Christian Phalange Party and part of the parliamentary majority led by the anti-Syrian March 14 coalition, was killed when explosives packed into a parked car detonated as his convoy passed through the Sin el-Fil district. Witnesses described a scene of devastation, with flames engulfing several vehicles and glass and debris scattered across the street.

The attack makes Ghanem the eighth anti-Syrian figure — and the sixth member of parliament from the ruling coalition — to be killed since 2005, when former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri was assassinated in a massive truck bombing that triggered the withdrawal of Syrian troops from Lebanon after a 29-year presence.

## Political Blame Game Erupts

Within hours of the blast, senior figures in the March 14 coalition pointed fingers at Damascus, accusing Syria of orchestrating a campaign of assassinations designed to intimidate lawmakers ahead of the presidential vote and erode the parliamentary majority needed to elect a president without Syrian and Hezbollah-aligned approval.

"This is a message written in blood, aimed at stopping us from exercising our constitutional right to elect a president," said Saad Hariri, leader of the parliamentary majority and son of the slain former premier, speaking to reporters outside his Beirut residence. "They want to empty parliament of its members one by one."

Syrian officials swiftly denied any involvement, with a Foreign Ministry statement in Damascus calling the accusations "baseless political exploitation of a tragedy." Hezbollah, the Iran- and Syria-backed group at the heart of Lebanon's opposition, also condemned the killing, with a spokesman describing it as "a criminal act aimed at further destabilizing the country."

## Presidential Vote in Jeopardy

The assassination strikes at the heart of Lebanon's most pressing political question: who will succeed President Emile Lahoud, a staunch Syrian ally whose term expires in late November.

Parliament had been scheduled to convene this month to begin the selection process, but the killing of Ghanem — whose vote was considered crucial to the ruling coalition's slim majority — has raised fears that the opposition may now be positioned to block a quorum or force a delay, deepening the constitutional standoff.

Analysts warn that further attrition of majority lawmakers could tip the balance of power in parliament, potentially handing the opposition, and by extension Damascus and Tehran, effective veto power over the choice of head of state.

"Every assassination changes the arithmetic," said a Beirut-based political analyst who requested anonymity given the sensitivity of the issue. "The message to the majority is clear: your margin is shrinking, and so is your room to maneuver."

## International Condemnation

The killing drew swift condemnation from the international community. U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice called the assassination "a cowardly attempt to derail Lebanon's democratic process" and reiterated Washington's support for the March 14 coalition. French President Nicolas Sarkozy's office issued a statement demanding an independent investigation, while U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon urged all Lebanese factions "to exercise restraint and allow constitutional institutions to function without intimidation."

The U.N.-backed international tribunal investigating Hariri's assassination, along with a related string of killings, is expected to examine whether Wednesday's bombing bears the hallmarks of the same network responsible for earlier attacks.

## A Nation on Edge

For many in Beirut, the bombing revived painful memories of the wave of violence that gripped the country between 2005 and 2006, when a string of car bombings claimed the lives of journalists, politicians and security officials critical of Syrian influence in Lebanon.

Shops shuttered early in several Beirut neighborhoods Wednesday evening, and security forces set up additional checkpoints across the capital. Army units were deployed to the blast site, where forensic teams combed through wreckage searching for clues.

"We keep burying our leaders one by one," said Marie Abou Rjeily, a resident of the nearby Achrafieh district who felt the explosion from her apartment. "How many more before someone finally answers for this?"

With the presidential deadline looming and the political majority now further diminished, Lebanon faces the prospect of a constitutional vacuum, raising fears of renewed instability in a country still scarred by civil war and foreign intervention.

Ghanem's funeral is expected to draw thousands of mourners and senior political figures in the coming days, an occasion that is likely to double as a show of defiance by the anti-Syrian coalition ahead of what promises to be one of the most contentious presidential contests in Lebanon's modern history.

*— Additional reporting contributed by wire services.*
